strengths: Introduces FIM-ODE, a pretrained foundation model for ODE vector field inference, applying amortized inference to ODEs with a neural operator architecture.

Demonstrates strong zero-shot trajectory reconstruction on ODEBench, outperforming ODEFormer across noise and subsampling regimes, despite being roughly 10x smaller and trained on about 80x fewer systems.

Provides a local neural operator representation as an alternative to global symbolic regression, with useful qualitative analysis of trade-offs on non-polynomial systems such as the pendulum and CDIMA reaction.
Shows pretraining can serve as a useful initialization for finetuning, enabling rapid adaptation and improved performance in some out-of-distribution settings.
Includes an extensive appendix with data generation details, architecture specifications, training hyperparameters, and additional experiments, which supports reproducibility.
Honestly discusses limitations, including the non-stationary polynomial prior, curse of dimensionality, and fixed state dimension.
weaknesses: The main results table includes 'FIM-ODE (Selected noise)', a cherry-picked favorable noise realization, which is not a legitimate method and can mislead comparisons; full 100-trial statistics in the appendix show much worse average zero-shot performance.

The abstract and conclusion overclaim that finetuned FIM-ODE 'outperforms modern neural and GP baselines'; in the VDP tasks it is worse than GP-DNF, LatentSDE, and others, and in MoCap it is not consistently best.

Zero-shot performance in low-data out-of-distribution regimes is substantially worse than classical baselines (e.g., VDP Task 1 MSE 0.89 vs. 0.03 for GP-DNF), weakening the zero-shot foundation-model claim.

Real-world human motion zero-shot results are catastrophic for some subjects (MSE 655 and 295), with only finetuning recovering reasonable performance; the 3D restriction also creates an uneven comparison and limits applicability.

Novelty is incremental: the architecture is adapted from FIM-SDE, and the framework/pretraining paradigm largely follows existing FIM work; the main contribution is applying it to ODEs with a polynomial prior.
The scope is limited to dimensions 1–3 and polynomial vector fields of degree at most 3, restricting significance for high-dimensional or non-polynomial real-world systems.

The code and model are not yet released despite the abstract promise, reducing immediate reproducibility; evaluation also lacks comparisons to classical methods on ODEBench (e.g., SINDy) and does not isolate the effects of prior, architecture, and data size.

strengths: Introduces FIM-ODE, a pretrained foundation model for ODE vector-field inference that amortizes inference into a single forward pass, extending the FIM framework to deterministic ODEs.

On ODEBench trajectory reconstruction (Table 1), FIM-ODE substantially outperforms ODEformer across all noise/subsampling settings (e.g., 84.4% vs 63.1% at sigma=0, rho=0; 72.1% vs 61.5% at sigma=0.05, rho=0.5), despite being about 10x smaller and pretrained on about 80x fewer systems.

The local neural-operator representation is an interesting alternative to global symbolic regression, and the paper gives a useful qualitative discussion of when local estimates can be advantageous (e.g., the CDIMA rational example).

Finetuning pretrained FIM-ODE can adapt to out-of-distribution low-data settings and real-world motion capture, yielding strong results in some cases (e.g., FHN MSE 0.04; MoCap subject 39 short 15.56).
The paper is generally well written and includes extensive appendices on data generation, architecture, normalization, and additional ablations, which aids understanding.
The limitations section honestly discusses the nonstationary polynomial prior, divergence issues, and the restriction to dimensions at most three, which is good practice.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction claim that finetuning 'outperforms modern neural and GP baselines' is not supported by the main tables. In Table 4, finetuned FIM-ODE is worse than GP-DNF and LatentSDE on VDP T1/T2 (0.16/0.26 vs 0.03/0.04 and 0.10/0.15). In Table 5, it is worse than GP-DNF/LatentSDE on several MoCap settings (e.g., subject 35 long: 11.73 vs 7.03/7.65; subject 39 long: 19.89 vs 16.21/18.72).

The main low-data tables include 'FIM-ODE (Selected noise)', a post-hoc best-noise realization. This is cherry-picking and not a legitimate method; the appendix shows the true zero-shot distribution is much worse (VDP T1 mean 0.575, median 0.340; FHN mean 1.871). Reporting this in the main table misleads readers.

There is a train-test mismatch: pretraining corrupts trajectories with multiplicative Gaussian noise, but the low-data VDP/FHN experiments use additive Gaussian noise. This likely explains poor zero-shot performance and makes the zero-shot comparisons unfair.

The MoCap comparison is not apples-to-apples: FIM-ODE is restricted to the first 3 principal components (remaining components set to zero) while baselines use 5D latent dynamics. This creates an information bottleneck, and zero-shot FIM-ODE catastrophically fails on subjects 35/39 (e.g., 655.40 MSE), undermining claims of real-world applicability.

ODEBench generalization (Table 2) shows FIM-ODE is only comparable to ODEformer, not better, so the 'match and often improve' claim is mostly limited to trajectory reconstruction. The frictionless pendulum example further shows failure to preserve conservative non-polynomial geometry.

The scope is very limited: pretraining is restricted to dimensions 1-3 and degree at most 3 polynomial vector fields. This excludes most realistic high-dimensional ODE systems and limits significance.
Reproducibility is incomplete: code/model/tutorials are not yet released, and it is unclear how many ODEBench systems with d>3 were excluded or how baselines were retrained for fair comparison.
Presentation/overclaiming: the abstract and contributions overstate zero-shot and finetuning performance; table typo 'RNeuralODE' and the selected-noise reporting reduce trust.

strengths: Introduces FIM-ODE, an amortized inference model for ODEs that extends the Foundation Inference Model framework to ordinary differential equations using a simpler polynomial prior and a neural operator representation.

Demonstrates that a local neural operator representation can outperform global symbolic regression (ODEformer) on trajectory reconstruction on ODEBench, and is competitive on generalization, despite being much smaller (8M vs 86M parameters) and trained on far fewer systems (0.6M vs 50M).

Provides a comprehensive set of experiments, including ODEBench, low-data out-of-distribution regimes (Van der Pol, FitzHugh-Nagumo), real-world human motion capture, and extensive ablations on discretization, dataset size, and vector field quality.
Shows that pretraining serves as a strong initialization for finetuning, enabling rapid adaptation to OOD systems and outperforming classical neural and GP baselines in several cases.
Includes detailed appendices with architecture, training, data generation, and additional results, supporting reproducibility and transparency.
Discusses limitations honestly, including the non-stationary prior, fixed dimensionality, and poor zero-shot performance in data-scarce regimes.
weaknesses: Zero-shot performance in low-data OOD regimes (Van der Pol, FitzHugh-Nagumo) is poor and often worse than classical baselines; the paper relies on finetuning or selected noise realizations to show competitiveness, which weakens the zero-shot foundation model claim.

On real-world MoCap data, zero-shot FIM-ODE fails catastrophically on subjects 35 and 39 (MSE in the hundreds) due to the 3D restriction and OOD dynamics; finetuning recovers performance but the method is not robust without adaptation.
The model is limited to state dimensions ≤3, which restricts its applicability to many real-world systems; the paper acknowledges this but it remains a significant limitation.

The novelty is incremental: the architecture is adapted from FIM-SDE, and the main contribution is applying it to ODEs with a polynomial prior; the comparison to ODEformer is not entirely apples-to-apples (different priors, model sizes, training sets).

The evaluation metric (fraction with R^2 > 0.9) on ODEBench generalization shows only small differences between FIM-ODE and ODEformer, with no consistent winner; statistical significance is not assessed.
Finetuning requires neural ODE training, which involves solver-based backpropagation and can be unstable and expensive, contradicting the claim of not requiring ML expertise.
The uncertainty weighting head adds 5M parameters (more than half of the total model) but no ablation is provided to justify its necessity.
The paper does not release code or pretrained models at the time of review (though promised), which hinders immediate reproducibility.

strengths: FIM-ODE achieves strong zero-shot trajectory reconstruction on ODEBench, outperforming ODEFormer across essentially all noise/subsampling settings (e.g., 84.4% vs 63.1% at σ=0, ρ=0 in Table 1) while being ~10x smaller (8M vs 86M params) and pretrained on ~80x fewer systems (0.6M vs 50M) from a much simpler polynomial prior.

The paper makes a clear and interesting conceptual point: a local neural-operator representation can match or beat global symbolic representations, and can transfer to OOD vector fields (trigonometric, rational) as long as the relevant state-space region is covered by context data (Tables 1-2, Table 10 ID/OOD split).

The interpretability analysis is a genuine contribution: inferred neural vector fields are queried for equilibria, Jacobians, and stability types (Figure 2, Table 13), and the CDIMA example shows FIM-ODE correctly classifying an unstable spiral where ODEFormer reverses stability despite finding a near-exact symbolic equilibrium.

The paper is transparent about its limitations and failure modes, including the frictionless-pendulum failure (centre misclassified as weak unstable spirals), the poor 3D ODEBench generalization (Table 10), and explicitly flagging the test-window checkpoint-selection caveat for the finetuned results (Appendix D.1).

Reproducibility is well supported: a pretrained model, code repository, and tutorials are released; data generation, architecture, normalization, and training hyperparameters are described in detail in Appendices B and C.
Ablations (dataset size, discretization, context size) and OOD tests on degree-6 polynomials provide useful context on scaling and robustness (Appendices F and G).
weaknesses: The headline finetuning results (FIM-ODE (Finetuned 2) in Tables 4 and 5) select checkpoints using the held-out evaluation window, which is not an independent test protocol. The training-loss-based alternative (Finetuned 1) is substantially worse and more variable (e.g., VDP T1 0.2(1) vs 0.028; VDP T2 0.4(3) vs 0.022), so the strongest reported numbers rest on a protocol the authors themselves acknowledge as non-independent.

Even after finetuning, the results do not uniformly dominate the classical baselines: on CMU MoCap (Table 5) FIM-ODE (Finetuned) is worse than GP-DNF on subject 09 (short 7.55 vs 7.03), subject 35 (short 6.92 vs 6.72), and on long horizons for subjects 35/39 (11.73 vs 7.03; 19.89 vs 16.21). The 'outperforms modern neural and GP baselines' claim in the abstract is therefore overstated.

The zero-shot regime is weak in low-data settings: FIM-ODE is far behind GP-DNF in Table 4 (0.90 vs 0.03 for VDP T1) and catastrophically fails on MoCap subjects 35/39 (655.4 and 295.3). Since adaptation (finetuning) is required in exactly the OOD cases of interest, the 'without requiring ML expertise' framing is weakened.

The scope is narrow: pretraining is restricted to autonomous polynomial vector fields of degree ≤3 and state dimension d≤3, with the maximum dimension hard-coded in the architecture. This limits applicability to most real scientific systems, and 3D ODEBench performance is already poor (16.7% reconstruction, 0% generalization).

The comparison to amortized baselines is incomplete: only ODEFormer is used as a pretrained baseline, omitting other amortized ODE inference methods cited in the related work (Becker et al., 2023; Şahin et al., 2025).

Some claims are supported only at relaxed thresholds. Trajectory generalization at R²>0.9 is broadly comparable to ODEFormer (Table 2), with the advantage appearing mainly at R²>0.8 (Table 12) or on median MSE (Table 11), which the abstract does not fully convey.

strengths: Timely and relevant direction: amortising ODE inference into a single forward pass is a useful goal, and the paper situates it well within the emerging FIM/simulation-based-inference literature.

Efficiency story is compelling: FIM-ODE (8M params, 0.6M pretraining systems) achieves clearly better ODEBench reconstruction than ODEFormer (86M params, ~50M systems), which is a concrete and non-trivial result.
The ID/OOD split analysis (Table 10) and the fixed-point/Jacobian diagnostics (Table 13, Figure 2) go beyond aggregate trajectory error and provide genuinely informative failure-mode analysis.
The paper is generally well written, and the limitations section honestly identifies the non-stationary prior, the d<=3 restriction, and the checkpoint-selection caveat in Appendix D.1.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: model, code, and tutorials are released, and the appendices document data generation, architecture, and training in detail.
Useful ablations on dataset size, discretisation, and context size (Appendices F and G) that characterise scaling behaviour and context sensitivity.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the FIM framework, the encoder-decoder neural-operator architecture, the transition features, the uncertainty-weighted loss, and the corruption scheme are all inherited from FIM-SDE/ODEFormer. The contribution is essentially a new polynomial prior plus a domain transfer, which is incremental.

Overstated central claims. 'Matching and often improving upon ODEFormer' holds for reconstruction (Table 1) but trajectory generalisation (Table 2) is essentially a wash (e.g. 29.5% vs 27.9% at sigma=0). The abstract's claim of 'outperforming modern neural and GP baselines' is only true for the finetuned variant, not the pretrained one.

Test-set leakage in the headline results. FIM-ODE (Finetuned 2), which beats GP-DNF in Table 4, selects checkpoints using the held-out evaluation window (Appendix D.1). The non-leaky variant (Finetuned 1) does not beat GP-DNF (0.2/0.4/0.06 vs 0.03/0.04/0.04). This materially weakens the strongest quantitative claim.

The interpretability claim is weak. Any differentiable neural vector field can be queried for equilibria, Jacobians, and stability; this is not a meaningful interpretability advantage over symbolic regression, and the diagnostics themselves show FIM-ODE misclassifying stability (pendulum centre turned into unstable spirals; LV equilibria distorted).

Zero-shot foundation-model performance is poor in the regimes that matter most: VDP forecasting MSE of 0.9 (vs 0.03 for GP-DNF) and MoCap subject 35 MSE of 655. This undermines the premise that a single pretrained model amortises inference; in practice it often requires finetuning, at which point the amortisation benefit is unclear.

MoCap comparison fairness is questionable: FIM-ODE is restricted to 3 PCA components while all baselines use 5, so latent dimensionality and information content differ across methods, confounding the comparison.

The pretraining objective is a pointwise MAE at sampled locations with no trajectory-consistency term, which plausibly explains the weak generalisation; this design choice is not ablated against a trajectory-based pretraining loss.

The prior's non-stationary scaling induces a curse of dimensionality (acknowledged) that caps the method at d<=3, which limits applicability to the higher-dimensional systems where amortisation would be most valuable.
There is at least one garbled/corrupted table in the reference material, suggesting production-quality issues in the compiled PDF.

strengths: The paper clearly formulates amortised ODE inference and adapts the Foundation Inference Model framework to ODEs, using a neural-operator/attention architecture to estimate the vector field locally from noisy trajectories in a single forward pass.

The proposed pretraining prior is simple and well-motivated: low-degree polynomial vector fields in dimensions 1-3. Despite this simplicity, FIM-ODE shows strong zero-shot reconstruction on ODEBench, often substantially outperforming ODEFormer, while being much smaller and pretrained on far fewer systems.

The interpretability analysis is a valuable contribution: inferred neural vector fields can be queried for equilibria, Jacobians, stability types, and phase-space geometry. The paper honestly discusses failure cases such as the frictionless pendulum and partially recovered Lotka-Volterra structure.

The experimental section is extensive, covering ODEBench reconstruction and generalisation, ID/OOD splits, synthetic polynomial systems, discretisation ablations, dataset-size scaling, low-data VDP/FHN tasks, and real-world MoCap data. Many baselines are compared.

Reproducibility is well supported: the model, code, and tutorials are stated to be available, and the appendices provide substantial detail on data generation, architecture, normalisation, training, finetuning, and hyperparameters.

The limitations and broader-impact discussions are thoughtful, including the nonstationary polynomial prior, dimension restriction, fixed-dimensional architecture, and risks of over-interpreting inferred vector fields.
weaknesses: The abstract and main text claim that finetuning 'outperforms modern neural and GP baselines', but this is mainly supported by FIM-ODE (Finetuned 2), which selects checkpoints using the held-out test MSE. The more honest FIM-ODE (Finetuned 1) does not clearly outperform GP-DNF or LatentSDE and has high variance. This caveat is only fully explained in Appendix D.1, so the central finetuning claim is overstated.

Zero-shot performance in the low-data OOD regime is weak and highly noise-sensitive; FIM-ODE is worse than several classical baselines on VDP forecasting and FHN imputation. This is acknowledged, but it limits the generality of the zero-shot inference claim.

The MoCap comparison is ambiguous: FIM-ODE is restricted to the first three PCA components while the baselines appear to use a five-dimensional latent representation. This may disadvantage FIM-ODE, but it also makes the comparison not fully apples-to-apples, and the zero-shot failures on subjects 35 and 39 are severe.

The pretraining prior is highly restrictive: autonomous, first-order ODEs with polynomial vector fields of degree at most three and dimension at most three. Many real scientific ODEs are higher-dimensional, non-polynomial, or non-autonomous, so the practical reach of the method is limited, even if this is discussed as a limitation.

On ODEBench trajectory generalisation, FIM-ODE is broadly comparable to ODEFormer rather than clearly better; at the stricter R^2 > 0.9 threshold it is sometimes worse. The 'matching and often improving' claim is therefore sensitive to task, metric, and threshold.

There is little ablation isolating the contribution of key architectural choices such as transition-based features, uncertainty weighting, and the local decoder. The interpretability diagnostics also rely on minimising ||f(x)|| to find equilibria, which can find spurious or distorted fixed points, although the paper reports residuals and some failure modes.

Presentation issues remain: the abstract overstates the finetuning results, the online link is not visible in the manuscript, and some table formatting and standard-deviation notation are ambiguous. These are minor but should be cleaned up.
